name: Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ)
place: Batanga Lohove grouping, Mboamanga chiefdom, Kribi (Océan, South)
overview: A fishing people of the Kribi coast, the Batanga came along the coast from the Nigeria-Cameroon border and keep ties with ndà-speaking peoples of Gabon, Equatorial Guinea and beyond. A minority among the Mabea, Bulu, Bakoko and Yasa, they live to the rhythm of the sea, the water spirits and the Mayi festival, which commemorates the return from exile in 1916.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Minority group, integrated with the Mabea, Bulu, Bakoko and Yasa.
Closely related speech varieties exist in the South-West (at the foot of Mount Cameroon), at Ngolo-Batanga and Penja-Batanga.
Formerly endogamous, the Batanga today marry more freely.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: Kribi was one of the first towns in the country to receive Christianity; people there also believe in water spirits and in Ndzambɛ ya Maɓenga.
Having come from the Congo and the Niger via the Nigeria-Cameroon border, the Batanga followed the coast as far as Lohote and Mahale (Kribi).
They maintain customary and cultural ties with Gabon, Equatorial Guinea and Mozambique, and linguistic ties with Ndà speakers.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: No kingship: clan chiefs were chosen for their management qualities; the chiefdom is now hereditary.
The family collectives, made up of heads of family, decide and inform the paramount chiefdom, which relays the message to all the villages.
Married men and age are respected, as a source of wisdom and experience; age groups (betuta) meet to share problems and experiences.
A married woman does not utter her husband's name: she invents another one for him.
There are old tensions with the Bakoko; with other peoples, peace reigns.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; the man goes to pay the bride price for the young woman in her village and then brings her back to his own.
A boy became a man when his father, with whom he fished, declared him so before everyone; he could then marry.
For the bride price, the young man fished and smoked the fish himself, proof of his abilities; his mother prepared the cassava sticks; palm wine was added. No fish, no bride price.
The elders then blessed the young couple by offering a bracelet.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: No ancestor worship; sacred sites exist but must not be revealed.
It is the other women, not the mother, who recognise in a newborn the return of a grandfather.
The deceased remains present: at events, his share of wine is poured out for him at the cemetery or around the house.
Incest is taboo; killing one's brother or wounding one's mother were the worst offences, left to the judgement of the water spirits.
Belief: what has been thrown into the sea is no longer looked at; that is why the houses on the shore did not face the sea.
The water spirits (nje ngu) speak through certain people.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: The man fishes in the morning then clears the field that his wife cultivates (cassava, plantain, cocoyam).
The land belongs to the clans, which redistribute it to families.
Ancestral crafts: dugout canoes, fish hooks, harpoons, tam-tams.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Men: wrapper and shirt, white suit on feast days; women: the large kaba dress.
People still heal with plants, such as ekukisani against malaria.
Beauty: codified hairstyles (a tuft in the middle of the skull for a married man, a long braid for chiefs, echoed in their hat); the woman with long hair and smooth, dark skin.
Courtship: the young man offered his fish, or a polished coconut on which he engraved a message; if the girl took it, the answer was yes.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Dances: àmbàsbé at major festivals, mbàyà in the moonlight, open to all; both enliven weddings.
Instruments: ngɔ̀mɔ̀ drum, struck bamboos mbàsí, mèkúlú tam-tam carved by canoe makers, dìbɛngɛ́ bell.
Festival: the Mayi, on 14 February and 9 May, commemorates the return to the ancestral land after the deportation of 1914–1916.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: Deported between 1914 and 1916, the Batanga were able to return to their land, which the Mayi commemorates.

sections.title: The names
items: Among twins (màváhá), the second to be born is the elder and bears the name of an elder brother of the father; the next child is called ebengi.
The parents choose the name freely, and it never changes.
At a certain age, an elder gives you a nickname that everyone adopts; “mola” means friend.
The founding ancestor, Mbɛ́ndì, bears the name of a chief fish of the estuaries, with pangolin scales, which dies only in the place where it was born.

lessons.title: Who are the Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ)? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • Minority group, integrated with the Mabea, Bulu, Bakoko and Yasa. • Closely related speech varieties exist in the South-West (at the foot of Mount Cameroon), at Ngolo-Batanga and Penja-Batanga. • Formerly endogamous, the Batanga now marry more freely. • Kribi was one of the first towns in the country to receive Christianity; people there also believe in water spirits and in Ndzambɛ ya Maɓenga. • Coming from the Congo and Niger via the Nigeria-Cameroon border, the Batanga followed the coast as far as Lohote and Mahale (Kribi).

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: A fishing people of the Kribi coast, the Batanga came along the coast from the Nigeria-Cameroon border and keep ties with ndà-speaking peoples of Gabon, Equatorial Guinea and beyond. A minority among the Mabea, Bulu, Bakoko and Yasa, they live to the rhythm of the sea, the water spirits and the Mayi festival, which commemorates the return from exile in 1916.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Power and social organisation among the Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ)
lessons.anelcac: Socio-political organisation, rules for living together
lessons.competence: Describe how the Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ) organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.
lessons.situation: An important decision must be made for the whole Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ) village. Who decides, and how?
lessons.materiel: The community's cultural profile, paper and felt-tip pens for the organisation chart.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe how the Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ) organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “An important decision has to be made for the whole Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ) village. Who decides, and how?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who holds authority? — How are decisions made (consensus, vote, the chief's decision)? — What rules of respect and deference are observed? — Which groups or societies play a particular role?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • No monarchy: clan chiefs were chosen for their management qualities; the chiefdom is now hereditary. • Family collectives, made up of heads of family, decide and inform the paramount chiefdom, which relays to all the villages. • The married man is respected, as is age, a source of wisdom and experience; age groups (betuta) meet to share problems and experiences. • The married woman does not say her husband's name: she invents another one for him. • There are old tensions with the Bakoko; with other peoples, peace reigns.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: No kingship: clan chiefs were chosen for their management qualities; the chiefdom is now hereditary. Family collectives, made up of heads of family, decide and inform the paramount chiefdom, which relays the information to all the villages. The married man and age, a source of wisdom and experience, are respected; age groups (betuta) meet to share problems and experiences.

steps.instruction: Draw a diagram (organisation chart) of power among the Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ), then explain in 3 sentences how a decision is made.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ)
objectives: Linking food to the living environment

vocabulary.langText: couscous de manioc, plantain pilé, mpɛlɛ́

lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ), describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ).
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ), describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ).” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: njaka (wild mango kernel sauce), ŋhluku (palm nut sauce), mokwa (spicy broth), cassava couscous, pounded plantain, mpɛlɛ́. • Drinks: mokwa, palm wine, coconut water. • The man fishes in the morning and then clears the field that his wife cultivates (cassava, plantain, cocoyam). • Land belongs to the clans, which redistribute it to families.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ) mainly eat njaka, ŋhluku, spicy broth, cassava couscous, pounded plantain, mpɛlɛ́. Traditional drinks: mokwa, palm wine, coconut water. These dishes are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Choose a dish of the Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ): write its sheet (name in the language, ingredients, steps, occasion when it is served).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.memo: Patrilineal kinship; the man goes to pay the bride price for the young woman in her village and then brings her back to his own. For the bride price, the young man fished and smoked the fish himself, proof of his abilities; his mother prepared the cassava sticks; palm wine was added. No fish, no bride price.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Leisure: traditional music and dances of the Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ)
objectives: Describe a dance and its instruments
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dances of the Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ), choose the most representative one, describe it, bring out its cultural significance and act it out.
lessons.situation: Taking part in cultural life in the family and in society: the class prepares a Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ) dance performance for the cultural day.
lessons.materiel: Instruments or recordings, costumes, clear space.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional dances of the Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ), choose the most representative one, describe it, bring out its cultural significance and perform it.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Taking part in cultural life in the family and in society: the class is preparing a Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ) dance performance for cultural day.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Which dances are practised, and on what occasions? — Who dances (men, women, children, initiates)? When and where? — Which instruments, songs and outfits are used? — What is the cultural meaning of the chosen dance?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Dances: àmbàsbé at major festivals, mbàyà in the moonlight, open to all; both enliven weddings. • Instruments: ngɔ̀mɔ̀ drum, struck bamboos mbàsí, mèkúlú tom-tom carved by canoe makers, dìbɛngɛ́ bell. • Festival: the Mayi, on 14 February and 9 May, commemorates the return to the ancestral land after the deportation of 1914-1916.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Among the Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ), traditional dances (major festivals, mbàyà) accompany the great moments of life: celebrations, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: ngɔ̀mɔ̀ drum, mbàsí bamboos, mèkúlú tam-tam, dìbɛngɛ́ bell. Festival(s): 14 February and 9 May.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Describe a Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ) dance (participants, time, instruments, gestures, meaning), then perform it with your group.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ)
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • The man fishes in the morning and then clears the field that his wife cultivates (cassava, plantain, cocoyam). • Land belongs to the clans, which redistribute it to families. • Ancestral crafts: canoes, fish hooks, harpoons, tom-toms.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The man fishes in the morning and then clears the field that his wife cultivates (cassava, plantain, cocoyam). Land belongs to the clans, which redistribute it to families.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a two-column table (men / women) of the Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ)'s activities, then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ)
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death

vocabulary.langText: regarder ce qu'on a jeté à la mer

lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ). Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ). Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • No ancestor cult; sacred sites exist but must not be revealed. • It is the other women, not the mother, who recognise in a newborn the return of a grandfather. • The deceased remains present: at events, his share of wine is poured for him at the cemetery or around the house. • Incest is taboo; killing one's brother or wounding one's mother were the worst offences, left to the judgement of the water spirits. • Belief: what has been thrown into the sea is not looked at again; this is why the houses on the shore did not face the sea.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: No ancestral cult; sacred sites exist but must not be revealed. It is the other women, not the mother, who recognise in a newborn the return of a grandfather.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ) (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

activities.title: I compare

student.memo: No ancestral cult; sacred sites exist but must not be revealed. It is the other women, not the mother, who recognise in a newborn the return of a grandfather.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Ɓanɔhɔ
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day

vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)
midday greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ) greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The community's language is Ɓanɔhɔ. • Greetings: Ǹlatò kɔ́hɔl = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); Mwàmó jámú = morning greeting (one person); Mwàmó jámú = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Jɔ̀hɔ́, Íɓà, ɓéláló, ɓénàjí, ɓétáno. • The founding ancestor, Mbɛ́ndì, bears the name of a chief fish of the estuaries, with pangolin scales, which dies only at the place where it was born. • Deported between 1914 and 1916, the Batanga were able to return to their land, which the Mayi commemorates.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Ɓanɔhɔ are the first steps towards communicating with the Batanga (Ɓanɔhɔ). Polite formulas express the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.
